    <item>
      <title>Braathen med ny maktdemonstrasjon: – Jeg er så full av følelser</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/sport/braathen-med-ny-maktdemonstrasjon_-_-jeg-er-sa-full-av-folelser-1.18082207</link>
      <description>Norsk-brasilianske Lucas Pinheiro Braathen (26) fortsetter å ydmyke konkurrentene.
Etter seier i storslalåm-starten i Sölden, fortsatte han med seier i slalåm i finske Levi søndag.
– Det er så godt å være her i Levi. Jeg er så full av følelser nå. Jeg skal prøve å ta selvtilliten med meg videre til neste renn, sier Braathen selv i arenaintervjuet.
Clément Noël ble nummer to, 56 hundredeler bak vinneren. Atle Lie McGrath ble beste norske på 7. plass.
– Det er hans bakke. Han elsker den. Han elsker disse forholdene, sier TV 2-ekspert Kjetil Jansrud på direkten.
– Han er fremdeles norsk, men han representerer Brasil. Vi skulle gjerne ha sett det norske flagget bak navnet hans, fortsetter Jansrud.
Dette er den tredje vinteren der Braathen representerer Brasil etter at han brøt med Norges Skiforbund.
– For en kjøring. Det er store, store avstander i en bakke som Levi, sa TV 2-ekspert Jansrud etter Braathens første omgang.
Han ledet med hele 65 hundredeler til toeren, Clément Noël, før finaleomgangen.

– Det Lucas gjør det er helt i egen klasse, sa Timon Haugan til TV 2 etter første omgang.
– Jeg fikk meg en på tygga, sier McGrath om finaleomgangen.
Oscar Andreas Sandvik kjørte seg opp fra 29. plass til nummer 11.
Både Timon Haugan og Henrik Kristoffersen tapte halvannet sekund til Braathen i første omgang. Begge fortsatte å skuffe i andre omgang og ble henholdsvis 18 og 19.
– Jeg kjørte i en stein, forteller Kristoffersen til TV 2.</description>

        <media:title>Bilder fra TV 2: Lucas Braathen med nok en seier i Levi</media:title>

    <item>
      <title>Vind og kaos-skyting: Kirkeeide vant fellesstarten etter åtte (!) bom</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/sport/vind-og-kaos-skyting_-kirkeeide-vant-fellesstarten-etter-atte-___-bom-1.18082184</link>
      <description>Maren Kirkeeide stakk av med seieren på kvinnenes fellesstart i skiskyting på Geilo søndag.
Lørdagens sprintsensasjon Guro Ytterhus imponerte igjen og tok andreplass 14,4 sekunder bak Kirkeeide.
Juni Arnekleiv ledet etter to fulle hus, men på tredje skyting ble det kaos. Sterk vind gjorde at flere av utøverne bommet mange ganger, og Arnekleiv røk på fire bom.
Dermed tok Karoline Knotten over teten. Men på siste skyting, så haglet skuddene utenfor blinkene nok en gang.
Og plutselig var Kirkeeide i tet etter hele åtte (!) bom. Få løpere måtte ut i flere strafferunder, men likevel holdt hun ledelsen helt til mål.
– Det var en merkelig fellesstart. Det var veldig mange som bommet. Det var tydeligvis ikke så lett som man skulle tro, sier Kirkeeide til NRK etter seieren.
Karoline Knotten tok tredjeplass.
Ingrid Landmark Tandrevold, Marthe Kråkstad Johansen, Karoline Knotten og nevnte Kirkeeide er forhåndsuttatt til verdenscupstarten i finske Kontiolahti senere i måneden. Kvinnenes tropp skal til slutt bestå av seks løpere.</description>

      <link>https://www.nrk.no/stor-oslo/kraftig-brann-i-lillestrom-1.18081998</link>
      <description>Det brenner kraftig i en enebolig på en gård i Trondheimsveien i Lillestrøm.
– Det er full fyr i hele bygningen, opplyser oppdragsleder i politiet, Ronny Mangseth.
– Brannvesenet er fremme og er i gang med slukking. Det er kontroll på alle fire beboere på stedet, sier han.
Ved 17:20-tiden opplyser politiet at det fortsatt brenner i boligen, og at arbeidet med slukking vil ta tid.
En person skal ha fått i seg noe røyk.
Det skal ikke være fare for spredning til låve eller andre bygninger på gården.
Ifølge politiet er det ikke kjent hva som er årsaken til brannen, og de vil etterforske saken videre.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Solbakken overrasker – Aasgaard inn i startelleveren</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/sport/solbakken-overrasker-_-aasgaard-inn-i-startelleveren-1.18081988</link>
      <description>Ståle Solbakken har valgt ut følgende ellever til kampen mot Wales på Ullevaal:
Egil Selvik – Julian Ryerson, Kristoffer Ajer, Torbjørn Heggem, David Møller Wolfe – Sander Berge, Martin Ødegaard, Thelo Aasgaard – Antonio Nusa, Erling Braut Haaland, Oscar Bobb.
– Jeg må innrømme at jeg er noe overrasket. Men da tenker vel Solbakken at han passer bedre til denne kampen enn det Patrick Berg gjør akkurat nå, sier NRK-ekspert Andrine Hegerberg om at Aasgaards inntog i startelleveren.
Han er én av fire bytter som er gjort fra elleveren som møtte Portugal i forrige nasjonsligakamp.
Leo Østigård, Andreas Schjelderup og Patrick Berg er henvist til benken, mens Fredrik Aursnes ikke er med på grunn av en skade.
Samtidig er det nok en gang Egil Selvik som skal vokte buret for Norge.
– Jeg er først og fremst stolt, men også spent. Det blir en viktig kamp for oss, så det gjelder å gi jernet. Vi har noe å revansjere, sier Selvik til TV 2.
På motsatt banehalvdel starter Wales med følgende mannskap:
Karl Darlow – Neco Williams, Joe Rodon, Ben Davies, Jay Dasilva – Harry Wilson, Ethan Ampadu, Liam Cullen, Daniel James – Lewis Koumas, Brennan Johnson.</description>

      <description>En eldre kvinnelig bilfører kjørte ned tre personer i Lyngdal.

      <description>Britisk politi bekrefter overfor BBC at de har innledet en etterforskning mot komikeren David Walliams for alvorlige seksuelle forbrytelser.

      <title>Thore «Henki» Holm Hansen er død</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/thore-_henki_-holm-hansen-er-dod-1.18081252</link>
      <description>Den tidligere Outlaws-sjefen og countrymusikeren er død, 82 år gammel, melder VG.
Holm Hansen ledet MC-klubben Outlaws, ble dømt for handel med narkotika og våpen og ga ut countrymusikk.
«Han sovnet stille inn på morgenen i dag, hjemme hos meg i sin egen seng, med venner og familie rundt seg», skriver datteren hans June Nordlie i et innlegg på Facebook.
Holm Hansen ble i 1981 dømt til 60 års fengsel i en kokainsak i USA, men ble besluttet deportert til Norge.
Selv hevdet han at dommen var et justismord, og knyttet saken til påstått arbeid for CIA.</description>

      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/over-144.000-norwegian-og-wideroe-passasjerer-rammet-av-datainnbrudd-1.18080740</link>
      <description>Informasjon om 144.249 passasjerer hos Norwegian og Widerøe er lekket i forbindelse med datainnbruddet hos den spanske IT-leverandøren Amadeus.
Det kommer fram i et brev Norwegian har sendt til Datatilsynet.
Fra før har SAS opplyst om at 350.000 av deres passasjerer er rammet.
Norwegian skriver at de fortløpende vurderer å varsle passasjerene.
Det var 27. oktober at datainnbruddet ble kjent. Innbruddet skal ha skjedd i 2023.</description>

   <description>Saudi-Arabiens Militärkoalition steckt im Jemen in der Krise. Während die Huthi vorrücken, zerfällt das Bündnis ihrer Gegner. Auch die Sicherheit einer wichtigen Handelsroute steht auf dem Spiel.</description>

Police are reminding e-scooter riders to know the rules of the road after an 80-year-old woman suffered serious injuries after reportedly being struck by a youth riding an e-scooter.

The post B.C. senior suffers serious injuries after being struck by youth on e-scooter appeared first on CHEK.

]]>

Police are reminding e-scooter riders to know the rules of the road after an 80-year-old woman suffered serious injuries after reportedly being struck by a youth riding an e-scooter.

The New Westminster Police Department (NWPD) says it was called to the parking lot area of 800 McBride Blvd. around 5:40 p.m. on Nov. 13 for a report of a pedestrian being struck by an electric scooter on a sidewalk.

When they arrived, police say they learned the elderly woman was exiting a Safeway in the area when she was struck by a youth on an e-scooter on the sidewalk.

“The impact knocked the woman to the ground, causing serious injuries,” said NWPD in a release Monday. “She was transported to Royal Columbian Hospital for medical treatment.”

Police say the incident serves as a reminder for the public about where and when micromobility devices, like e-scooters, can be ridden.

Currently, e-scooters are only permitted through a pilot project in some B.C. communities – with New Westminster not numbered among them, meaning it’s illegal to ride an e-scooter anywhere in the municipality, including on public roads and sidewalks.

In general, it’s illegal to ride e-scooters on sidewalks anywhere in the province, including in communities that have signed on to the pilot program.

“Riders should be aware of the applicable laws and the significant safety risks associated with improper use,” said NWPD. “Officers have the discretion to stop and share information with e-scooter riders, or in some cases, issue a ticket.”

The police department says tickets can include a $598 fine for operating an unlicenced and uninsured vehicle.

The NWPD says it continues to investigate the crash between the youth and the senior. It notes that the youth remained at the scene and their parents also attended.

The e-scooter was seized as part of the investigation and police are also reviewing surveillance video of the area. Anyone with information on the crash who has not yet spoken with police is asked to call the New Westminster Police Department at 604-525-5411 and quote file 26-19657.

“The New Westminster Police Department would also like to thank the members of the public who stopped to assist the injured woman while emergency services were en route,” said the NWPD.

A full list of communities participating in the e-scooter pilot project can be found on the Province of B.C. website. Several neighbouring communities to New Westminster are part of the project, including Burnaby, Coquitlam, Vancouver, North Vancouver and Richmond.

On Vancouver Island, 15 communities are part of the pilot program, including Victoria, Langford, Nanaimo, Oak Bay, Ladysmith and more.

]]> 1361860 National Congress of American Indians calls on Trump to reverse Lake Ontario change https://cheknews.ca/national-congress-of-american-indians-calls-on-trump-to-reverse-lake-ontario-change-1361853/ Tue, 17 Nov 2026 17:15:00 +0000 https://cheknews.ca/?p=1361853

The National Congress of American Indians is calling on U.S. President Donald Trump to walk back his August executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.

The post National Congress of American Indians calls on Trump to reverse Lake Ontario change appeared first on CHEK.

]]>

The National Congress of American Indians is calling on U.S. President Donald Trump to walk back his August executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.

The organization, which represents American Indian and Alaska Native tribal governments in the United States, says the order disrespects Indigenous geographic names and Indigenous cultural, spiritual and historical relationships with lands and waters.

A resolution rejecting the name change, passed at the organization’s October assembly, was introduced by the Seneca Nation of Indians, a community based in western New York.

Trump directed all arms of the federal government to start calling the body of water Lake America in August, to the dismay of Haudenosaunee communities whose languages are the source of the name “Ontario.”

In Seneca, Lake Ontario means “beautiful lake,” and in Wendat it means “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.”

The resolution says unilateral efforts to rename geography risk erasing Indigenous history and calls on the U.S. federal government to suspend its use of the term “Lake America.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

]]> 1361853 Measles is no longer considered eliminated in the US and Mexico https://cheknews.ca/measles-is-no-longer-considered-eliminated-in-the-us-and-mexico-1361850/ Tue, 17 Nov 2026 17:00:00 +0000 https://cheknews.ca/?p=1361850

The U.S. has lost its measles-free status as the highly contagious virus once relegated to medical textbooks has spread. Last year, Canada lost its measles-free designation for the first time since 1998.

The post Measles is no longer considered eliminated in the US and Mexico appeared first on CHEK.

]]>

The U.S. has lost its measles-free status, international health officials said Tuesday, as the highly contagious virus once relegated to medical textbooks has spread — largely among the unvaccinated — at the highest rate in more than 30 years.

Mexico also lost its measles-elimination status, following a resurgence of the virus there that included a massive outbreak in Chihuahua state. Bolivia, too, lost its status.

The Pan American Health Organization declaration has few practical implications and is largely symbolic, but it marks a sharp turnabout in a disease largely controlled through decades of scientific advances. It also may be seen as the beginning of an era in which diseases of the past become deadly problems for the modern world.

“Measles elimination is not a trophy that is won once and placed on a shelf,” said Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO’s director. “It is an achievement that must be safeguarded every day by closing immunity gaps and ensuring we reach every community.”

Measles has been spreading throughout the Americas since 2024. The outbreaks in North America started in close-knit Mennonite communities and have since spread to areas with low vaccination rates. Last year, Canada lost its measles-free designation for the first time since 1998.

RELATED: Measles outbreak over after 2 years, thousands infected in Canada: PHAC

International health officials consider measles eliminated when the virus is not locally spreading among residents. The designation hinges on whether a single measles chain has spread uninterrupted for at least 12 months.

Tuesday’s announcement signals an erosion of public health preparedness.

Vaccination rates have been falling against a number of diseases, in the U.S. and globally. And as one of the most infectious diseases known to medicine, measles was seen as likely to be one of the first vaccine-preventable diseases to re-emerge when vaccinations falter.

That means others are likely to follow, some experts said.

“It can be the canary in the coal mine to other things,” said Dr. Susan Kansagra, chief medical officer of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials.

Vaccine rates fall and cases go up

Measles vaccines have safely stopped the virus’ spread in the U.S. for 30 years.

It takes a community vaccination rate of 95% to prevent outbreaks, experts say. But as fewer parents vaccinate their children and federal leaders sow doubt and confusion about the importance of getting vaccinated, the virus has found footholds in communities across the U.S. All but three states have reported a confirmed case of measles this year.

“This humiliating determination is the tragic yet predictable result of an ongoing campaign by grifters, quacks and charlatans to put their own greed and self-worth ahead of the health and safety of children,” said Sen. Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon.

The last two years have been the worst in a generation in the U.S., with more than 7,000 cases and 11 deaths. Nearly all of those people were either unvaccinated or didn’t report whether they were vaccinated. More than 10% of those infected had to be hospitalized.

The illness typically begins with a high fever followed by a telltale rash that starts on the face and neck. Most people recover, but it’s one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization. Serious complications, including blindness and swelling of the brain, are more common in young children and adults over age 30.

Ten measles-associated deaths have been reported in the U.S. this year. Health officials have not released detailed information on each death, but at least five of the dead were children.

This year’s measles death count is higher than what has been seen in any previous year in more than three decades.

And the U.S. is experiencing its worst year for measles illnesses since 1991.

The U.S. has seen major outbreaks in Texas, Utah, South Carolina and Pennsylvania

Since the U.S. eliminated measles in 2000, public health officials usually logged less than 200 cases a year, most of them tied to international travel.

But since 2025, measles has sickened thousands. It started with a major outbreak in the southwest.

In Texas, more than 760 people got sick and two children died. And in New Mexico, about 100 people got sick and one adult died.

In the summer of 2025, measles exploded in extremely rural border towns in Arizona and Utah. And a major outbreak in South Carolina in the winter and spring sickened nearly 1,000 people to become the fastest growing measles outbreak the nation has seen in decades.

Bad as 2025 was, this year has been much worse. The more than 5,400 confirmed cases so far this year are already double the 2025 tally, driven largely by an outbreak in Pennsylvania that has dwarfed the earlier ones.

And the outbreak tallies are almost certainly an undercount, public health experts say.

Critics say the US response is falling short

U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has no formal medical training, was a leading voice in the anti-vaccine movement before President Donald Trump appointed him to oversee federal health agencies.

Kennedy and other federal leaders have argued that vaccination rates were waning for years before Trump took office a second time, that measles is not an “American phenomenon,” and that the U.S. government is handling measles better than other countries. In January, a CDC leader told reporters that the loss of the nation’s elimination status would be the “cost of doing business” globally.

It’s true that other countries are struggling with measles, and some also have lost their measles-elimination status. But some experts say the outcome in the U.S. wasn’t inevitable.

The government has been taking some steps. In August and September, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention awarded $100 million — in two tranches — to support state and local measles-response work. And Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz have made statements that vaccination is the best way to prevent measles from spreading.

But state and local health officials say the cost is far higher than that.

“It wasn’t a lot of money, frankly,” said Chrissie Juliano, executive director of the Big Cities Health Coalition, which represents three dozen of the largest U.S. city health departments.

Experts also say the moment demands a louder federal voice — and a bigger push for vaccinations — than Kennedy and Schwartz are providing. Some noted that neither Kennedy nor the CDC has scheduled a news conference for this week to address how they plan to try to regain measles-elimination status.

“When the people at the front of the room are not speaking loudly and frequently in support of vaccination, the program starts to falter. And that’s what we’re seeing in the U.S.,” said Noel Brewer, a University of North Carolina public health professor who chairs a committee that presented an analysis of U.S. measles data to PAHO last week.

“The federal government has had such a ho-hum response,” he said. “How many kids have to die before they start getting concerned?

What’s next?

After hugely successful vaccination campaigns, the Americas became the first region in the world to be free of measles in 2016. Health officials estimate the measles vaccine prevented 6.2 million deaths in the Americas between 2000 and 2023.

Now, the entirety of North America faces the task of earning back the designation.

Some individual countries have achieved, lost, and then regained measles-elimination status. Brazil is one example. Another is the United Kingdom, although it lost its status a second time — this year.

]]> 1361840 A dementia diagnosis is devastating. What happens when you’re only 48? https://cheknews.ca/a-dementia-diagnosis-is-devastating-what-happens-when-youre-only-48-1361831/ Tue, 17 Nov 2026 16:30:00 +0000 https://cheknews.ca/?p=1361831

Mark Breslaw sat in his car at a four-way stop just minutes from home, but suddenly didn't know which way to turn.

The post A dementia diagnosis is devastating. What happens when you’re only 48? appeared first on CHEK.

]]>

Mark Breslaw sat in his car at a four-way stop just minutes from home, but suddenly didn’t know which way to turn. 

“It was like I blinked and I opened my eyes and I didn’t know where I was. I had no recollection of how I got to this particular position and the worst feeling was I didn’t know what to do and there’s people lining up behind me,” recalledthe 50-year-old former human resources executive.

“I just thought the safest thing is just to go straight, which wasn’t actually what I was supposed to (do),” said Breslaw, who had been driving the same route from work to his home in Surrey, B.C., for 18 years.  

“I didn’t get far before I went, ‘OK, there’s the elementary school. I know I’m close … and then I was back.”

Although he was scared, Breslaw didn’t tell his wife what had happened when he got home that day three years ago, because he didn’t want to alarm her. He also didn’t connect the memory lapse to some problems that he — normally a very high performer in a fast-paced job — had been having at work. 

Sometimes he would forget the names of people he worked with every day. Other times he couldn’t remember what floor he was taking the elevator to. Usually an excellent planner, he was finding tasks like scheduling his week took far longer than they used to. Once he missed three back-to-back meetings.

“None of this was constant and so, you know, it would happen and you’d be like ‘that was weird.’ But then it would happen again, maybe a week later, two weeks later,” Breslaw said.

He was worried, but chalked it up to stress, lack of sleep and a busy life balancing work with raising a young son. He also has two grown children who live on their own. 

But when he found himself lost at that four-way stop two more times, he made an appointment to see his family doctor in January 2024. 

What he thought would be a quick discussion turned into a long process that resulted in a diagnosis neither he nor his doctor expected: young-onset Alzheimer’s disease. 

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common type of dementia, which is the umbrella term for a group of diseases that damage brain cells. Although it most often affects older adults, dementia is not a normal part of aging.   

An estimated 772,000 people live with dementia in Canada and could grow to a million by 2030, the Alzheimer Society of Canada says. 

Dementia is defined as “young-onset” when it is diagnosed in someone under 65 years old.  It’s relatively rare — a 2024 report by the society estimates there were about 28,000 people living with young-onset dementia in Canada in 2020. It projects that number will reach more than 40,000 by 2050.

“Gathering accurate statistics on young onset dementia in Canada is … complicated by the fact that currently there is no national system for tracking all cases of dementia more broadly, let alone for people who develop dementia under the age of 65,” the report says.

A dementia diagnosis is devastating for anyone, but younger people face specific issues and services often don’t meet their needs, said Cathy Barrick, CEO of the Alzheimer Society of Ontario.

“These are people who are often in the prime of their life. They’re still working. They may have children still at home. They may have children in university,” she said.

“The very first service that is the biggest challenge is actually (getting) a diagnosis. So, I mean, diagnosis is challenging for dementia at any age, but even more so at a younger age because it is so not assumed that that is the problem.” 

That was Breslaw’s experience during visits with both his family doctor and a neurologist. 

“You’re too young to have dementia, essentially, was the message,” he said.

He went through a series of tests and scans looking for brain tumours, evidence of stroke, depression, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder — anything that could explain his symptoms. 

Even when he scored lower than expected for his age on a cognitive test, his neurologist still didn’t think dementia was likely.

Finally, about a year after he first went to his doctor, a cerebrospinal fluid test revealed the amyloid beta protein that is a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease. 

Breslaw was 48 years old.  

FAMILY AND FINANCES

Immediately, Breslaw had to give up his driver’s licence because he now had spatial impairment. He also had to leave the career he loved, because his doctor explained the work would quickly become too complex to manage as his disease progressed. 

He and his wife pushed through their shock and grief to take control of anything they could, from seeing a financial planner to picking out a cemetery plot.   

People with Alzheimer’s disease can live for 10 years or more and have a good quality of life with the right supports, said Saskia Sivananthan, CEO and co-founder of the Brainwell Institute, a dementia think-tank. 

Although there is no cure, there are a few medications approved by Health Canada that can help manage symptoms or slow the rate of progression — but each individual case is different and patients need to discuss the risks and benefits with their doctor.

The disease is ultimately fatal as it progresses through different parts of the brain and eventually affects control over breathing, swallowing and other bodily functions, said Sivananthan, who is a neuroscientist. 

Developing dementia while they are still young often forces patients and their families to figure out how to deal with the unexpected loss of income, she said. 

Breslaw’s wife, now 46, has a senior job she loves at a local hospital foundation. He said he wants her to continue working full-time rather than taking time off to be his caregiver — not only because of the financial need, but because she has an identity that extends beyond his illness. 

They worry about what they’ll have to spend as Breslaw needs more and more care, as they want to make sure their eight-year-old son has money for post-secondary education in the future. 

“These are the things that we have to think about. You get diagnosed at 48, you immediately go into all the what-if scenarios,” he said. 

LONG-TERM CARE VS HOME CARE 

Breslaw’s family also figures prominently into where he wants to receive round-the-clock care when he needs it.

“I hear … people who are younger want to stay at home longer and I believe that to be very true for many people. It’s not true for me because I have an eight-year-old son,” he said. 

“I don’t want it to look like a hospital and kind of see dad in that sort of very vulnerable way.”

Breslaw would rather move into a long-term care home to spare his family. 

“I’m going to be largely surrounded by people who are, you know, two and a half decades older than me, if not older than that.”

His ideal living situation would be a transition house that could keep younger people who can no longer function on their own safely, but also allow them to have a better quality of life than in long-term care.   

That’s an area where young-onset dementia support is definitely lacking, Sivananthan said. 

“Most long-term care or assisted living places are not really set up for him. They are set up for older adults.”

DEMENTIA DAY PROGRAMS

Almost two years after his diagnosis, Breslaw can still walk his son to school and stay home while his wife is at work. 

But he can no longer use the stove or microwave after doing so “almost led to a very catastrophic fire in our house.” 

He was warming up some food for what he thought was 30 seconds but was actually 30 minutes and then walked away to fold laundry. 

Breslaw forgot about the microwave altogether until the kitchen was full of smoke. 

He knows as his Alzheimer’s disease progresses, he may need to go to a day program. They are available in many communities, but mostly designed for older people in their 70s, 80s and 90s, Breslaw said. 

Barrick, of the Alzheimer’s Society, said someone with young-onset dementia may actually find that experience confusing if they are in later stages of the disease.  

“He may be like, ‘why am I here with all these old people? Like, this is weird, I should be at work. Where is my wife?'” she said. 

“As his brain changes, he may not be able to put those pieces together. And so it can actually create some behaviours that get exhibited in programs like that, because they can become quite distressed.”

Breslaw, who volunteers for the Alzheimer Society of British Columbia and Yukon, is part of a “small and mighty group” of people with young-onset dementia that advocates for more resources, such as transition houses, age-appropriate day programs and guidance on how to talk to children about what lies ahead. 

MAID

The federal government recently announced it planned to amend the Criminal Code to allow people with dementia to make advance requests for medically assisted dying (MAID) before they lose their mental capacity to do so. 

Those requests would lay out specific conditions when they would reach the point of intolerable suffering and want MAID to be administered, such as deterioration to the point where they don’t recognize their family.  

But it’s up to the provinces to decide if their health-care systems will honour advance requests. 

B.C. has not announced a position yet.

Breslaw doesn’t know whether or not he would make an advance request if it’s allowed, but saidknowing it’s an option would give him peace of mind. 

“It literally is something that keeps me up at night and it would be a weight lifted off my family just to have the choice,” he said.

Five staff members are leaving the office of Opposition Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, including his deputy chief of staff and two of his senior communications aides.

Poilievre’s deputy chief of staff, Aaron Wudrick, confirmed he told his colleagues last week he had accepted an opportunity in the private sector and will be leaving his position on Nov. 27.

“I want to thank all of you for your co-operation and hard work in our shared mission to make Pierre Poilievre our next prime minister leading a Conservative government, and remain fully confident that this goal remains achievable in the next election,” he said in an email to the Conservative caucus and Poilievre’s office. 

“I will miss life on Parliament Hill and working with all of you, but am looking forward to a new challenge that will allow me to spend more time with my family.”

Wudrick is leaving after nearly three years in the role.

Media relations director Sam Lilly is departing after spending six years working in the Opposition leader’s office, including since Poilievre became leader in 2022. Lilly said he is moving to British Columbia to join the new provincial Conservative government that is being sworn in later this week.

“My roots are in British Columbia. It’s where I grew up, graduated high school, joined the military and formed some of my fondest family memories,” said Lilly. “After a wonderful career that has taken me across our great country, it is time to come home and be a part of the team that will build British Columbia’s brightest days ahead.

“Pierre has made a difference to this country, he continues to have my support and I know that our team will continue the work of ensuring he is the next prime minister of Canada.”

Poilievre’s office also confirmed CBC and CTV reports that communications director Micah Green is also joining the B.C. government, and that executive assistant Hayley Quipp and senior policy adviser Andrew Evans are also both leaving.

These departures signal a significant shakeup in Poilievre’s inner circle and come after the departures of longtime chief of staff Ian Todd in May, and former communications director Katy Merrifield, who left to return to B.C. in April.

Merrifield was the campaign director for the B.C. Conservatives in the recent provincial election, which saw that party oust the NDP from government, after former premier David Eby called a snap election.

The latest departures also come just a few weeks before voters head to the polls in six federal byelections in Quebec, Ontario and Saskatchewan.

Wudrick joined Poilievre’s team as a policy adviser in 2024, and moved into the deputy chief of staff role in May when Todd announced his retirement. When he started, the Conservatives were well ahead of the Liberals in the polls and appeared poised to win a large majority government in the next federal election.

That lead evaporated in a matter of weeks in the winter of 2025, after former prime minister Justin Trudeau announced his departure and Mark Carney joined the race to replace him. Carney won that contest and led the Liberals to a minority government in April 2025, the fourth consecutive election loss for the Conservatives.

A year later, Carney turned his minority into a majority, luring one NDP and four Conservative MPs to join his caucus. The Liberals also turned a fifth Conservative seat red earlier this year, winning a byelection in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord, after Quebec MP Richard Martel resigned to take an appointment to the Senate.

The federal Conservatives have continued to drag in the polls well behind Carney and the Liberals, who have built a significant lead as he shepherds Canada’s response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs and threats of annexation.

Evans joined the Opposition leader’s office around the same time as Wudrick, while Quipp has been Poilievre’s executive assistant since June 2023. Green has been part of Poilievre’s communication team since 2022, and was promoted to director in April, when Merrifield departed.

A Catholic school in Surrey, B.C., is praying that Jesus will help a group of thieves after they stole a life-size copper statue of Christ from the school’s courtyard. 

Silveria Roselli, president of the Saint John Paul II Academy Foundation, said the school community was “very distraught” to learn of the theft early in the morning on Nov. 11, when three people drove through a fence in a white van and cut the statue off at the knees.

“Some of the kids were very much devastated. It was like a death in the family,” Roselli said in an interview on Monday.

Roselli said one of the students suggested it was possible the thieves needed to find Christ, and she was praying Jesus would help them find what was missing.

“We hope that whoever did this will repent and that will bring Jesus back home,” said Roselli. 

“As a school, we pray for them that they will find God and find Jesus.”

The theft was caught on the school’s security camera and has been shared on social media, but police have said the van used by the thieves was also stolen.

“An extensive initial search for suspects or a suspect vehicle was negative,” Surrey police said in a statement.

Police said officers received a report of the theft on Nov. 11 and visited the school to speak to staff and gather evidence.

“We understand this incident is impactful to the school and their community,” they said. “The investigation is ongoing.” 

Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson condemned the theft, describing it as a “disgraceful act against a community of faith and a school.”

“To the students, families and staff at the Academy: we stand with you,” he said on social media, urging anyone with information about the theft to contact police.

Roselli said the school would be boosting its security.

“We’re working with the police, and we will not let evil prevail,” she said.

The statue, entitled “The Last Supper,” depicted Jesus sitting before a plate and cup on a table, surrounded by 12 empty stools. It was donated by Canadian artist Timothy Schmaltz.

Joseph King, chair of the Saint John Paul II Academy Society, said the statue was an invitation for students, teachers and guests to sit and contemplate themselves as apostles of Christ and consider receiving the eucharist.

King said it was also a “beautiful” place to study or have lunch. 

Roselli said the statue would be replaced as soon as possible with help from a fundraising effort.

A GoFundMe page, launched by Saint John Paul II Academy Foundation, asks people to help bring Jesus home. 

“While the sculpture was made of copper, its true value was never in the metal, but in what it represented: the love of Jesus Christ and his presence among us,” the page said.

While the theft had left a sense of emptiness at the courtyard, Roselli said hearts in the community were full after seeing the support they’re receiving.

“It’s mainly beautiful to see the love, support of the community,” she said.

Police say members of the local search and rescue team were deployed after authorities learned the group had found one person safe, but a 29-year-old woman from Squamish was still missing.

The woman was eventually found downstream and died at the scene.

It was the fourth death in as many days in waters near the community, where three people died after a boat overturned in the swollen Squamish River on Thursday.

To the southeast, police say there’s an ongoing search for a 60-year-old man missing since a boat overturned in the Fraser River near Yale on Friday.

RCMP say officers from the Hope detachment responded to a report of a man floating in the river and yelling for help that afternoon.
